Remember the distinction: Firefighters suppress fires and rescue people, while Fire Inspectors And Investigators identify hazards. One responds on the front line and the other prevents incidents at the source.

A common path is recruitment as a Firefighter, academy training, front-line response, crew responsibility, and then fire captain or incident commander.
This career suits brave, resilient people who collaborate in extreme conditions. Firefighting can be a stable path if your standard is getting people out safely.

paragraphs: During standby, Firefighters train and inspect equipment. When an alarm sounds, they gear up and deploy. On scene, they lay hoses, raise ladders, search for victims, judge structures in smoke, handle hazardous materials and injuries, clear the site, and review the response.

In one sentence: rescue people from fires. The work includes receiving alarms, suppressing fires, conducting searches and rescues, handling hazardous materials, operating equipment, and reviewing incidents. It requires both judgment and physical action on the city's front line.

Low-moderate exposure does not mean high career risk. Systems replace the act of watching reconnaissance feeds, not structural judgment and rescue roles. Firefighters who judge conditions and save lives become scarcer as productivity rises. Feed-only reconnaissance roles face the greatest risk.
Start with physical testing and emergency-response training. Practice teamwork and first aid. Pure reconnaissance is shrinking in the AI era, so develop judgment early.

Highlight physical-test results and service history. State which emergencies you have handled. Fire services value steadiness and courage.
Do not select people on fitness alone. Test judgment as well. Firefighters who can lead rescues merit advancement.
